newsitem.title: USA: White House, lawmakers edge toward budget deal.
newsitem.headline: White House, lawmakers edge toward budget deal.

text.p: President Clinton and Republican lawmakers edged closer Wednesday to a five-year plan for balancing the federal budget and cutting taxes and a key senator said he hoped it would be concluded soon.
Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici told reporters he was exchanging budget information with the White House and hoped to know soon whether an agreement would be possible this week.
"We'll know something pretty soon," the New Mexico Republican said. Asked if a budget deal might be possible this week, Domenici replied, "yes."

The two sides have been negotiating in secret for weeks on a plan to bring the deficit down to zero by 2002. The size of a tax cut, the depth of spending cuts and the president's request for some new programmes have been the major divisions.
The White House was still insisting on new spending for education and other domestic initiatives, Republicans said.

Clinton has said he hoped to conclude an agreement prior to his departure Monday for Mexico. His spokesman, Mike McCurry, said while talks had been "good and productive," it was uncertain whether differences could be worked out by then.
In any case, House Democrats said they were resisting the idea of a quick deal and would prefer to take more time to negotiate a deal to their liking.

House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri praised Clinton's effort to balance the budget but said Democrats were wary of a budget deal that might hurt the Medicare health care for the elderly and wanted to see tax cuts targeted to the middle class.
"We're not going to be for a bad deal. No deal is better than a bad deal. We've got to be careful about what's agreed to here," he said at a news conference.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, who predicted a deal would be reached yesterday, told reporters, "I still think we're very close, it won't be a perfect agreement from any viewpoint, but we are relatively close."

His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Tom Daschle of South Dakota, told reporters he found reports by White House officials of the negotiations "comforting." But he warned that Republican efforts to change the way spending bills were approved would jeopardise reaching an agreement.
The chief tax writer in the House, Ways and Means chairman Bill Archer said they were "pretty close on the tax side."

He told reporters "it would be nice" if budget negotiators agreed on a net $100 billion in tax reduction over a five-year period, this would be roughly five times Clinton's original net tax cut offer.
Archer, a Texas Republican, said a tax deal had to accommodate a broad-based capital gains reduction and significant improvement in estate taxes. He called for action on the alternative minimum tax.

When the White House presented this plan to Democrats late Tuesday they again found resistance. The tax proposal offered by Republicans would balloon to $250 billion in the second five years and would either raise the deficit or force cuts in spending to pay for it.
Clinton recommended a $98 billion tax cut chiefly focused on education, child tax credits and would be paid for with $76 billion in other tax hikes for a net tax cut of $22 billion.
